title: Remember Me, Refine Me: A Dynamic Procedural Memory Framework for Experience-Driven Agent Evolution
problem_statement: Existing procedural memory frameworks treat experience as a static append-only archive, causing the pool to degrade into valid insights mixed with toxic noise over time. No existing system addresses the full lifecycle: high-quality extraction, task-grounded utilization, and progressive optimization with principled deletion.
key_ideas: Multi-faceted distillation: three complementary analyses (success pattern recognition, failure analysis, comparative insight generation) extract structured keypoint-level experiences from trajectories
Structured experience format E = <ω, e, κ, c, τ> (usage scenario, content, keywords, confidence, tools) indexed by LLM-generated usage scenario embeddings
Context-adaptive reuse: top-K retrieval + LLM reranker + LLM rewriter that produces cohesive task-specific guidance
Utility-based refinement: selective addition (success-only), failure-aware reflection (failed trial → new attempt → add if succeeds), and utility-based deletion (u/f < β after f ≥ α retrievals)
Memory-scaling effect: smaller model + ReMe outperforms larger model without memory
method_summary: ReMe operates through three alternating phases: Experience Acquisition (LLMsumm distills N=8 trajectory samples into structured experiences via success/failure/comparative analysis, validated by LLM-as-judge, deduplicated by cosine similarity), Experience Reuse (top-K=5 retrieval by usage scenario embedding similarity, optional reranking and rewriting), and Experience Refinement (selective addition of successful experiences, failure-aware reflection, utility-based deletion when u/f < β=0.5 after α=5 retrievals). No fine-tuning; fully prompt-based. LLMsumm = LLMexecute in main experiments.
metrics: Avg@4 (average task success rate across 4 trials)
Pass@4 (probability at least 1 of 4 trials succeeds)

key_results.selective_vs_full_addition: Selective addition +3.50% Avg@4, +2.66% Pass@4 over full addition
key_results.best_retrieval_key: Usage scenario indexing > generalized query > query keywords > task query
key_results.dynamic_vs_fixed: Dynamic refinement consistently outperforms fixed memory pool
key_results.stronger_summarizer: Qwen3-32B LLMsumm with Qwen3-8B LLMexecute: +3.33% Avg@4 vs. self-summarization

contributions: ReMe framework integrating multi-faceted experience distillation, context-adaptive reuse, and utility-based refinement
Fine-grained keypoint-level experience extraction (vs. trajectory-level) with structured E = <ω,e,κ,c,τ> format
Failure-aware reflection mechanism for learning from failures without polluting the experience pool
Utility-based deletion for progressive memory optimization
reme.library: fine-grained procedural memory dataset with success patterns and failure lessons
Empirical demonstration of memory-scaling effect: smaller model + memory > larger model without
limitations_acknowledged: Fixed retrieval strategy: experiences retrieved only once at task start, not dynamically mid-task
LLM-as-judge validation may overlook nuanced quality dimensions
Larger-scale summarizer improves performance but increases compute cost
limitations_observed: No cross-domain transfer tested between benchmarks
No analysis of experience pool evolution over time (quality plateau, optimal pool size)
Latency overhead not fully analyzed beyond the +2.54s/task reported for AppWorld
Main experiments use only Qwen3 family; cross-family generalization limited to Figure 3
relevance_to_thesis: Directly relevant to all three focus areas. Memory Controller: provides complete implementable schema E=<ω,e,κ,c,τ> with lifecycle management including utility-based deletion. Educability: failure-aware reflection and comparative insight generation operationalize structured learning from contrast. Knowledge Transfer: memory-scaling effect directly demonstrates procedural knowledge compensating for parameter count; stronger summarizer experiment shows cross-capability knowledge extraction.
gaps_and_questions: Can experiences from a stronger model bootstrap a weaker model's performance? (extends Table 5 to cross-model transfer)
How does the experience pool evolve over many tasks — does quality plateau or degrade?
Can a single cross-task experience pool generalize better than task-specific pools?
Can utility thresholds α and β be learned or adapted per domain?
Would a two-level hierarchical experience structure (abstract principle + concrete step) improve generalization?
poc_ideas: Implement ReMe experience structure as procedural memory layer in thesis memory controller; test utility-based deletion vs. simple LRU
Test memory-scaling effect with cross-model summarizer: use larger model to extract experiences, smaller model to execute
Build cross-domain memory pool spanning multiple task types and measure transfer vs. task-specific pools
Compare ReMe and MemP (2508.06433) directly on same benchmark to understand complementary design choices
